Exaltation is about being lifted high — either in feeling, in status, or in glory. Everything this word does, it does with intensity and grandeur. Think of it as the noun form of "exalting" something or someone, which means to raise it to the highest possible level — whether that's raising a person to a throne, raising someone's spirit to the heavens, or raising your own feelings to a peak of joy.

1. An Overwhelming Feeling of Joy and Triumph

This is the most common, everyday use of the word. Exaltation is not just happiness — it is happiness cranked all the way up. It is the kind of soaring, almost disbelieving joy that floods through you in a moment of great triumph, achievement, or beauty. Your whole being feels elevated, like you are floating above the ordinary world.

Examples of when you might feel exaltation:

  • A runner crosses the finish line of a marathon they trained for years to complete. The feeling that crashes over them is exaltation.
  • A scientist who has worked a decade on a cure finally sees it succeed. That rush of overwhelming, tearful joy is exaltation.
  • Standing on a mountain peak at sunrise and feeling a surge of pure, breathtaking emotion — that is exaltation.

It is important to understand what makes exaltation different from regular happiness or excitement:

  • Happiness is a general, steady good feeling.
  • Excitement is energetic anticipation or enthusiasm.
  • Elation is close to exaltation — it is strong joy — but exaltation carries an extra layer of grandeur and intensity. Exaltation feels almost spiritual or divine. It is the kind of joy that can make you feel like crying, like you are part of something bigger than yourself.
  • Ecstasy is similar too, but ecstasy tends to suggest a loss of control. Exaltation is more noble and uplifting — a soaring of the soul rather than being swept away.

2. The Act of Raising Someone to a High Rank or Position

Exaltation can describe the act of officially lifting a person to a powerful, prestigious, or honored position. This is a more formal use, often found in historical, political, or religious writing.

Examples:

  • The exaltation of a warrior to the status of king — the ceremony, the crowning, the moment of elevation.
  • A saint's exaltation — being officially declared holy and raised to a position of divine honor.
  • In a company or organization, someone's exaltation to a leadership role.

Here, exaltation is not just a promotion. It carries a sense of public recognition, ceremony, and greatness. It implies that the person being raised up is worthy of that high place.

3. The State of Being Praised, Glorified, or Held in High Esteem

Closely linked to the meaning above, exaltation can describe the condition of being treated as extraordinary, superior, or magnificent — being placed on a pedestal by others.

Example:

  • The poem spoke of the exaltation of nature — treating the natural world as something almost divine and beyond compare.
  • The speech was full of the exaltation of human courage and sacrifice.

Here, exaltation is about the glorification itself — the high regard in which something or someone is held.

In Religion

Exaltation carries deep, specific meaning in religious traditions.

  • In Christianity, "the Exaltation of the Holy Cross" is an actual feast day that commemorates the glorification of the cross as a sacred symbol. More broadly, the exaltation of Christ refers to his resurrection, ascension to heaven, and glorification — being raised to the highest divine status.
  • In Latter-day Saint (Mormon) theology, exaltation is a very specific term. It refers to the highest possible state of existence in the afterlife — becoming like God in the highest degree of heavenly glory. It is the ultimate spiritual achievement a person can reach.
  • In general spiritual language, exaltation describes the state of a soul being lifted to closeness with the divine — a transcendence beyond the ordinary human experience.

In Astrology

In astrology, a planet is said to be in exaltation when it is positioned in the zodiac sign where it is considered strongest, most powerful, and most able to express its qualities in the best possible way. For example, the Sun is said to be in exaltation in the sign of Aries. It is the opposite of being in its "fall," which is its weakest position.

As a Collective Noun

In a beautiful and poetic quirk of the English language, an exaltation of larks is the official collective noun for a group of larks (the birds). Just as you say "a flock of birds" or "a pride of lions," you say "an exaltation of larks." This phrase was recorded as far back as the 15th century. It was chosen because larks are known for soaring high into the sky and singing beautiful, joyful songs as they rise — a perfect image of exaltation.
The Register and Tone of This Word

Exaltation is not a word you would use in casual, everyday conversation. It belongs to a higher register of language — formal writing, literature, poetry, religious texts, and moments where you want to express something grand and significant. If you use this word, you are signaling that what you are describing is not ordinary. It has weight, majesty, and importance.

You would not say: "I felt exaltation when I ate a good sandwich."

You would say: "She felt a sudden exaltation as the orchestra swelled and the lights flooded the stage."
A Single Summary to Lock It In

Exaltation is the noun that captures anything that has been — or feels — raised to the highest level. It is the soaring, overwhelming joy of a supreme moment. It is the formal elevation of a person to greatness and glory. It is the glorification of something held in the highest regard. And in specific contexts, it is the strongest position of a planet, the highest state of spiritual existence, or simply a beautiful word for a group of singing, sky-bound birds.

Whenever you see or hear exaltation, think: lifted high, intensely glorious, beyond the ordinary.
